939.title: Leo XIV (2025)
939.hook: Robert Prevost, an Augustinian from Chicago who served in Peru, becomes pope and greets the world with peace
939.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the pope by name in the Eucharistic Prayer at Mass, and after an election the new pope's name is added to those prayers in churches around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the conclave: cards carried to the altar, ballots burned, a crowd watching a chimney. Your line was white smoke.

Peace be with you all. Those were the first words, spoken in Italian, by a new pope at the microphone on the balcony of Saint Peter's. Not about himself, or the vote, or the job. A cardinal had just announced him: Robert Francis Prevost, who had taken the name Leo. He grew up in Chicago. He spent years as a missionary in Peru. And he belongs to a religious order named for a bishop of North Africa, Augustine of Hippo.
screen: `FIRST WORDS: PEACE BE WITH YOU ALL.` → `A NEW NAME: LEO.` → `CHICAGO, PERU, AUGUSTINE.`

segments.voice: First, those words. Leo said this was the greeting of the risen Christ. He was pointing at a scene in John's Gospel. On the evening of the first Easter, the disciples are hiding behind shut doors, afraid, and Jesus comes and stands in the middle of them. In the Douay-Rheims his first words are simply: "Peace be to you." No blame for running away. Peace first. Second, the man. Robert Prevost joined the Order of Saint Augustine, friars who live in community under Augustine's rule. He went to Peru as a missionary, later served as bishop of Chiclayo, in the north of the country, and became a Peruvian citizen. On the balcony, after Italian, he switched to Spanish to greet his old diocese by name. Third, Augustine. In that first speech he quoted his order's founder, who once told his congregation, in effect, that for them he was a bishop, but with them he was a Christian. Augustine's point, as Leo used it: the man in white is first of all one more baptized person in the crowd. Fourth, the name. Speaking to the cardinals in the days after, Leo explained he chose it partly for Leo the Thirteenth, the pope who wrote about the dignity and rights of workers when factories were remaking the world. Leo said the Church faces another such revolution now, in artificial intelligence, and wants to speak to it in the same spirit.
screen: `PEACE: THE RISEN CHRIST'S GREETING.` · `CHICAGO, PERU, AND THE AUGUSTINIANS.` · `FOR THEM A BISHOP, WITH THEM A CHRISTIAN.` · `A NAME FOR A CHANGING WORLD.` · then, large: `PEACE BE TO YOU.`

segments.voice: In the Eucharistic Prayer at Mass, the priest prays for the pope by name, and now that name is Leo: say it once, slowly, and think of what the job asks of one person, to speak for peace, to hold together a Church spread across the world, to get up tomorrow and do it again. If you pray, pray for him by name, in your own words or in silence; if you don't, hold him in mind the way you would anyone with a heavy job.
Leo the Fourteenth. Robert Prevost of Chicago, an Augustinian friar and a missionary bishop in Peru, elected pope, who greeted the world with peace.

940.title: Carlo Acutis (1991–2006)
940.hook: a teenager who built a website on Eucharistic miracles, now a canonized saint
940.howItsDone: Catholics visit Carlo Acutis's tomb in Assisi, keep his feast, and in some parishes show his exhibit on Eucharistic miracles; some young Catholics ask his prayers for their life online.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo the Fourteenth, a friar from Chicago by way of Peru, whose first words were for peace. Your line was peace be with you all.

A teenager in Milan sits at the family computer, teaching himself to code. He isn't building a game. He's building a website. Country by country, he gathers accounts of Eucharistic miracles, stories of the bread and wine of the Mass tied to wonders, and lays them out as panels anyone could print and hang up. The same boy makes silly films with his pets, and rations his own video games so they don't take over. His name was Carlo Acutis, and the Church now calls him a saint.
screen: `A TEENAGER TEACHES HIMSELF TO CODE.` → `A WEBSITE OF EUCHARISTIC MIRACLES.` → `NOW CALLED A SAINT.`

segments.voice: First, the ordinary part. People who knew him remember a boy in jeans and sneakers, good with computers, who stuck up for classmates who were picked on and stopped to talk with homeless people near his home. Second, the website. He believed, as the Catholic Church teaches, that Jesus is truly present in the Eucharist, and he wanted people to notice. So he spent his spare time building an online exhibit of Eucharistic miracles, the way another kid might build a fan site. It has since been printed and shown in parishes far from Milan. Third, his line. Carlo used to say the Eucharist was his highway to heaven, and those around him say he went to Mass whenever he could, every day if possible. The image was a teenager's own; the text behind it is older. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." As his family tells it, his days were built around that sentence. Fourth, his other remembered saying: everyone is born an original, but many die as photocopies. He died young, of leukemia, offering his suffering, those with him said, for the pope and for the Church. He is buried in Assisi, where pilgrims file past his tomb, and he was canonized together with Pier Giorgio Frassati, another young layman. Carlo didn't flee the internet or drop his friends, some Catholics point out. He used the tools in front of him to point at what he loved.

segments.voice: Picture your phone and the last few things you did on it, no guilt, just noticing, then choose one small good thing it could be for: a kind message, a true and beautiful thing shared, a search for a food bank or a parish near you. If you pray, offer your screen time to God the way Carlo offered his; if you don't, let this minute be quiet and unscrolled.

941.title: The Jubilee of Hope (2025)
941.hook: a holy year of pilgrims of hope
941.howItsDone: In a jubilee year, Catholics make pilgrimages to Rome or to churches their bishop designates, pass through holy doors, go to confession and receive Communion, and pray for the pope's intentions to receive the jubilee indulgence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carlo Acutis, the teenager who called the Eucharist his highway to heaven. Your line was the eucharist, my highway.

A crowd moves slowly down the long avenue toward Saint Peter's. Parish groups in matching shirts. Families pushing strollers. An old man with a cane, keeping up. Across the city, inside a Roman prison, another group keeps the same holy year without leaving the building, because the pope came to them and opened a holy door there. Both groups are pilgrims. Their year has a name and a motto: the Jubilee of Hope. Pilgrims of hope.
screen: `A CROWD ON THE LONG AVENUE.` → `A HOLY DOOR IN A PRISON.` → `PILGRIMS OF HOPE.`

segments.voice: Jubilee starts in the book of Leviticus, where the Hebrew word is yovel. There God tells Israel to count off the years and then keep a special one: land goes back to the families who lost it, and people who had to sell themselves into service go free. In the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt sanctify the fiftieth year, and shalt proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land: for it is the year of jubilee." Remission means release, a debt let go. The Church borrowed that idea. Tradition holds that the first Catholic holy year was declared in the Middle Ages, and since then popes have proclaimed them from time to time, with pilgrims receiving an indulgence, the Church's word for a release from the punishment still due for sins already forgiven. Francis gave this jubilee its theme in a document called Spes non confundit, Latin for hope does not disappoint, a line of Saint Paul to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "hope confoundeth not." Paul gives the reason straight after: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts. A pilgrim isn't a tourist. A tourist goes to see something. A pilgrim goes to be changed on the way: the walking, the waiting, the sore feet, the prayer at the end. The jubilee asked Catholics to travel as pilgrims of hope, to Rome or to a church in their own diocese set aside for the year, and, in the old spirit of Leviticus, to let something go. Partway through, the pope who opened it died; a new pope carried it on.
screen: `YOVEL: A YEAR OF RELEASE.` · `HOLY YEARS IN THE CHURCH.` · `HOPE DOES NOT DISAPPOINT.` · `A PILGRIM IS CHANGED ON THE WAY.` · then, large: `FOR IT IS THE YEAR OF JUBILEE.`

segments.voice: A pilgrimage doesn't need a plane: picture a walk to a place nearby that means something, a church, a cemetery, a bench where someone you loved used to sit. Decide what you'd carry on the way, a hope or a worry, and what you'd set down when you arrive. If you pray, pray as you walk; if you don't, let the walking itself be the attention.

942.title: The world Church
942.hook: the Catholic Church's center of gravity shifts toward Latin America, Africa and Asia
942.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the same Mass in many languages and musical styles, and some parishes in Europe and North America are served by priests and religious sisters from Africa, Asia and Latin America.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jubilee of Hope: pilgrims on the long avenue, and a holy door opened inside a prison. Your line was pilgrims of hope.

Some Sunday mornings now look like this. In a small town in the American Midwest, the priest at the altar grew up in Nigeria. In a parish in Ireland, the homily comes in the accent of southern India. In Kinshasa, a choir comes up the aisle dancing, with drums. In Manila, the doors are open because the crowd won't fit inside. And in Rome, the last two popes came from Buenos Aires and from a missionary life in Peru. Same Mass, same prayers, many languages.
screen: `A NIGERIAN PRIEST IN THE MIDWEST.` → `DRUMS IN KINSHASA.` → `POPES FROM THE AMERICAS.`

segments.voice: The Creed at Mass calls the Church catholic, and the Catechism says plainly what that means: universal. A church for everyone, everywhere. For long stretches of history, though, the center of Catholic life sat in Europe: its bishops, its universities, the missionaries it sent out. That picture has changed. Writers who follow the Church describe its center of gravity moving south, toward Latin America, Africa and Asia, and they point to the Church's own yearly statistics to show it. Catholics read their oldest texts as pointing this way from the start. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus sends the apostles out: "Going therefore, teach ye all nations." And at Pentecost, in Acts, the crowd in Jerusalem is Jews gathered from far and wide, "devout men, out of every nation under heaven," each hearing the apostles in his own language. Some readers call Pentecost the Church's birthday: a church that spoke many languages on its first day. The shift isn't a tidy story. In some places the faith arrived with missionaries who traveled alongside colonial powers, and that history includes real harm, which the Church has had to face. But the faith also spread through local catechists, mothers and grandmothers, and converts who made it their own and sang it to their own music. Today the traffic runs in every direction: African and Asian priests serve European parishes, Latin American theologians are read in seminaries far away, and bishops from every continent sit together at synods in Rome.

943.title: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church
943.hook: an Eastern Catholic church outlawed under Soviet rule that survived underground
943.howItsDone: Ukrainian Greek Catholics celebrate the Byzantine Divine Liturgy in Ukrainian and other languages, in Ukraine and in parishes abroad, and honor the bishops, priests and laypeople who were imprisoned or killed under Soviet rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world Church: on every continent, its center of gravity moving south. Your line was the church moved south.

A small apartment in Soviet Ukraine, late at night, the curtains drawn. A laborer takes a folded cloth from a drawer, spreads it on the kitchen table, and sets out bread and a cup. A few neighbors come in quietly, one at a time, so no one notices a crowd. He is a priest, and this is the Divine Liturgy, sung almost in a whisper. Accounts from those years describe scenes like this. Officially, his church does not exist.
screen: `CURTAINS DRAWN, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A KITCHEN TABLE FOR AN ALTAR.` → `A CHURCH THAT DOESN'T EXIST.`

segments.voice: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church worships the way Orthodox Christians in Ukraine do: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, married men among its parish priests. And it is in full communion with the pope. Greek in its name means the Byzantine tradition, not the country. It is one of the Eastern Catholic churches, which keep their own rites and their own laws while belonging to the one Catholic Church. After the Second World War, Soviet authorities set out to erase it. Its bishops were arrested. A gathering held under state pressure declared the church dissolved and its parishes joined to the Russian Orthodox Church. Priests who refused were sent to labor camps. Its head, Metropolitan Josyf Slipyj, spent years in the camps before he was released to Rome. But the church didn't vanish. It went into kitchens, forests and cemeteries. Bishops were ordained in secret; priests held ordinary jobs and served at night. Grandmothers baptized babies quietly and taught the prayers at home. Catholics read those years through a promise in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." A kitchen table was enough. As Soviet rule loosened toward its end, the church came out of hiding, and its people filled their churches openly again. It's a story with wounds on more than one side: Orthodox believers suffered under the same regime, and churches in Ukraine still carry that history together. But the underground church kept the Liturgy going in the dark until it could sing it in daylight.

944.title: Catholics under pressure today
944.hook: in some countries Christians practice their faith at real risk
944.howItsDone: Catholics pray for persecuted Christians in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, some parishes light their churches red on a day of remembrance, and charities support communities under pressure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the underground church: a Liturgy at a kitchen table, until it could be sung in daylight. Your line was the underground church.

Open an old calendar of martyrs and the scenes come easily: arenas, emperors, ancient Rome. Then open the news. In Nicaragua, a Catholic bishop, Rolando Álvarez, is sentenced to prison and later sent out of the country. In Nigeria, a parish in the town of Owo is attacked during Mass on Pentecost Sunday. In other places, believers meet quietly, because meeting openly could cost them a job, their freedom, or more. Those stories are still going on.
screen: `AN OLD CALENDAR OF MARTYRS.` → `A BISHOP IN PRISON, THEN EXILE.` → `A PARISH ATTACKED AT MASS.`

segments.voice: The Church calls those killed for the faith martyrs. It keeps their names, and it is still adding to them. The Acts of the Apostles tells of one of the earliest: Stephen, one of seven men the community chose to serve at its tables, stoned for what he preached. As the stones fall, he prays for the men throwing them, asking the Lord not to hold this sin against them. The Gospel never promised otherwise. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Pressure isn't treated as a sign that something went wrong. It's named ahead of time. Then there's remembering. The letter to the Hebrews asks its readers to remember prisoners as if they were in chains alongside them, and those who suffer as people living in the same kind of body. That is one reason Catholics in a quiet suburb pray for a parish in Nigeria or a bishop far from home: in that letter's picture, they are not strangers in a headline. And pressure now? Sometimes it is violence. Often, those who track it say, it is quieter: laws that close schools and charities, a job lost after a baptism, a priest followed by police, a church that can never get a building permit. Believers of other faiths face it too, and the Second Vatican Council taught that religious freedom belongs to every person. Some parishes light their buildings red on a chosen day, red for the martyrs. Others read names aloud at Mass, so they are not forgotten.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catholics under pressure today: a bishop sent into exile, a parish attacked at Mass, names said aloud. Your line was not only long ago.

Trent, in northern Italy, during the Second World War. The bombs are falling, and a young schoolteacher named Chiara Lubich crowds into an air-raid shelter with a few friends. They've brought one book, the Gospels, and read it by candlelight, asking what would still stand if everything else fell. They keep landing on Jesus's prayer that his followers may all be one. Years later in Rome, high school students start meeting to read the Gospel, then going out to the poor on the city's edge. Neither group was started by a bishop or a priest.
screen: `A BOMB SHELTER IN TRENT.` → `ONE BOOK BY CANDLELIGHT.` → `STUDENTS IN ROME.`

segments.voice: Chiara's circle became the Focolare movement. Focolare is Italian for hearth, the fire a family gathers around, and that was the idea: small communities living the Gospel together like a family at the fire. Their key text is Jesus's prayer at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." Focolare took it to heart, building friendships with other Christians, with people of other faiths, and with people of none. The Roman students, gathered by Andrea Riccardi, took their name, Sant'Egidio, from a small church in the Trastevere neighborhood. Their life rests on three things: prayer each evening, friendship with the poor, and peace. That last one reached all the way to a war: talks held at their house in Rome helped bring the civil war in Mozambique to an end. Who leads? These movements are led by laypeople, people who aren't priests or vowed religious, with jobs and families. The Second Vatican Council taught that the laity share in the Church's mission by their own calling, through baptism, not as helpers on loan from the clergy. Movements like these are one shape that teaching took. Priests and bishops belong to some of them, but the founders were a teacher and a student. Look back over the week: a pope greeting the world with peace, a teenager with a website, pilgrims, a church on every continent, a church underground, believers under pressure, and now laypeople leading. One Church, through different doors.
